newsitem.title: USA: U.S. farm price index dips in December.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farm price index dips in December.

text.p: Lower prices for wheat, corn, oranges, cattle and milk pushed the farm price index down by 1.8 percent during December, the U.S. Agriculture Department said Monday.
The index, a gauge of prices paid to farmers for their crops and livestock, had a December reading of 108, down from 110 in November but unchanged from a year ago.
Wheat dipped 12 cents to average $4.02 per bushel, and was 86 cents below the December 1995 price. The department said projected increases in world wheat output caused prices at home to fall.
Meanwhile corn prices were driven lower by the third largest U.S. crop on record, ringing in at $2.56 per bushel, off 10 cents from November and 51 cents from December 1995.

Milk prices continued to decline after hitting a record high in September, easing to $14.20 in December, down 80 cents from November. The department said cheese and butter prices also continued to weaken.
Orange prices dropped to $3.54 per box from $4.07 garnered in November, while lemons plunged to $6.60 per box from $8.01 the prior month, the department said.

Beef cattle prices averaged $60.70 per 100 pounds in December, down $2.50 cents from the preceding month but 10 cents higher than one year earlier. Hog prices were unchanged at $54.40 per 100 pounds but were $10.90 above last year.
Among the farm goods that saw price gains in December, the department said soybeans, at $6.92 per bushel, increased 2 cents from November.
"Expected tighter supplies at the end of the marketing year has been the major factor in the price increase," the department said. Prices for peanuts and cottonseed were also up from last month.

Broilers climbed by 7 cents to 41.6 cents per pound and eggs rose 5 cents to 87.7 cents per dozen, but turkeys fell 1.8 cents to 43.6 cents per pound. The department pointed to continued strong export demand for all poultry and egg products.
